detail: The two resulting versions of the scene can be drawn in succession using shuttered glasses synced with the monitor, or drawn simultaneously using stereo viewers [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the two resulting versions of the scene can be drawn in succession using shuttered glasses synced with the monitor, or drawn simultaneously using stereo viewers. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'The two resulting versions of the scene can then be drawn in succession using shuttered glasses synced with the monitor to render the stereo effect. Alternatively, left and right versions of the scene may be drawn at the same time using stereo viewers to reveal the stereo effect.' The claim is fully supported by the evidence.
Stereo projection applies a perspective projection twice with adjustments to simulate the viewpoint for an observer's left and right eye, creating a stereo effect [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that stereo projection applies a perspective projection twice with adjustments to simulate the viewpoint for an observer's left and right eye, creating a stereo effect. Source [S1] explicitly states in section 2.1.3: 'A stereo projection is simply a perspective applied twice making adjustments to simulate the viewpoint as seen for an observer's left and right eye... to render the stereo effect.' The evidence directly supports every part of the claim.
The specific implementation described here is referenced in the context of the Smokeview tool for visualizing fire dynamics simulation data [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the specific implementation (stereo projections) is referenced in the context of the Smokeview tool. The provided evidence explicitly discusses 'Stereo Projections' in section 2.1.3 and immediately follows with section 2.1.4 'Viewports' which mentions 'Smokeview' and Figure 2.5 illustrating 'a typical Smokeview scene'. The context of the document is clearly about Smokeview, and the stereo projection details are part of this context.
It generates two correlated view frustums rather than one [S1, unofficial].

The source text explicitly states in section 2.1.3 that 'A stereo projection is simply a perspective applied twice making adjustments to simulate the viewpoint as seen for an observer's left and right eye' and that 'Figure 2.4 illustrates the two view frustums used for a stereo projection.' This confirms that the process generates two view frustums (one for each eye) rather than one.
